rv.q: Betty Blue Eyes, apart from being a blatant plug for Spam, will be welcomed by all animal lovers and piggy aficionados.
With this superbly endearing and entertaining show, producer Cameron Mackintosh has once again brought home the bacon.
But this witty and delightful adaptation of the 1984 film A Private Function strikes me as better than the original.
Composer George Stiles and lyricist Anthony Drewe have written a series of charming songs, with nostalgic lilt and literate rhyming that explain the effect Betty Blue Eyes has on stout-hearted men.
A portrait of Britain in an age of austerity and insidious inequalities isn't obvious material for a musical comedy.

The 1940s cheer us up no end: no sooner have we warmed to the camaraderie of 1941 in Flare Path than we get this romping musical version of 1947: in which two American writers, Ron Cowen and Daniel Lipman, adapt Alan Bennett's tale of snobbery, skulduggery and illegal pig-raising for ‘a private func...

Producer Cameron Mackintosh has put the whole thing together with splendid panache, Eyre’s fine work supplemented by the fluently conceived, picturesque designs of Tim Hatley and the witty choreography – making the most of queues, victory marches and processions – of Stephen Mear .
Betty Blue Eyes is the equivalent of a proper Sunday roast - pork, of course, not beef.

This likeably performed and technically accomplished musical has some welcome moments that make the audience squeal with laughter, plus a few that may have them grunting impatiently for the next scene to arrive.

cn.t: Critics embrace Betty Blue Eyes as a witty, charming delight, with several calling it superior to Alan Bennett's source film. Its satirical warmth and irresistible porcine star win consistent praise across the board.
